messages.subject_clean: LAI Variable in Microclimate Model
messages.body_plain:
If I may be able to pitch in a bit: from my experience using the NMR microclimate model and interfacing with microclima, and from discussions with Ilya, for the microclima sides of things LAI is one of the more important parameters for determining amount of intercepted downwelling radiation. But my hunch would be the same, that for a low veg desert system you probably don’t need to worry too much. I can’t recall off the top of my head if it’s been built into microclima functions/calls to these functions via micro_global or micro_era5, but in the microclimc package there are lists of default veg parameters for a set of categorical habitat types (eg for you could be barren or short grassland) that would provide estimates of LAI. You can take a look at these via microclimc::LAIfromhabitat(), or microctools::LAIfromhabitat (I’m currently in the field and don’t immediately recall which one).

Hope this helps,
Dave

> All the best,

> >

> > Thank you!

Hi Adam - in the endotherm model, TC_MAX is the maximum it allows the body temperature to go as part of its thermoregulatory response. By implication, if all other options are exhausted and the predicted metabolic rate remains below basal, then the animal would have overheated past the the TC_MAX and died.
All the best,
Mike

messages.subject_clean: How to feed different temps into environ
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

It's hard to know what's wrong without some example code. The ectotherm model expects input tables called metout, soil, shadmet and shadsoil which by default are passed in as e.g.:
 metout = micro$metout

So you can either alter micro$metout before calling the ectotherm model or make your own metout table and pass that in directly. You may already know this, but the environ table is what the organism is exposed to and will vary depending whether th organism is above or below ground.

Here is an example of how to override e.g. TALOC to be a constant 40 deg C:

library(NicheMapR)

micro <- micro_global()

ecto <- ectotherm()
environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(environ$TC, type = 'l')

micro$metout[, 3] <- 40 # change TALOC, column 3, to 40 deg

ecto <- ectotherm()
environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(environ$TC, type = 'l')

All the best,
Mike

Hi Alex,

You were changing the values correctly but the main issue is how you set up the microclimate model. You specified the reference height the same as the local height - you shouldn't change the reference height as it is referring to the height the macroclimate data (air temp, wind speed, humidity) were recorded at. I really shouldn't have made it an option to change in the micro_ functions. Also, the depths must be roughly similar to the defaults, going to about 2m maximum and spaced logarithmically, i.e. the spacing increasing with depth. Finally, you selected 'runshade = 0' which you shouldn't do if you're running the ectotherm model, which expects two shade scenarios as input, i.e. from metout and shadmet, soil and shadsoil, etc.

I think you'll find once you've fixed those issues with the microclimate model, it should all make sense. E.g. run it like:
micro <- micro_global(loc = longlat, timeinterval = timeinterval, soiltype = 5, elev = 961, runmoist = 0, nyears = nyears, runshade = 1, minshade = 0, clearsky = 1, run.gads = 1, IR = 0, soilgrids = 0, Usrhyt = 0.005, slope = 0, aspect = 0, REFL = 0.15)

Note some of the ectotherm model parameter settings you've specified are not needed if you're not running the DEB model. I.e. CTKILL onwards in your list.

All the best,
Mike

> > >
> > > It's "TC". Operative temperature is the 'steady state' temperature some object would reach if held indefinitely in a given environment, and this is essentially what the model is predicting. It's the same as what you'd get with a low heat capacity physical model of the organism, e.g. one made of copper, so it changes temperature almost instantly as the environment changes (e.g. as the sun comes out from behind a cloud). I.e. it isn't accounting for the object lagging behind the temperature its environment is driving it towards, because of rapid changes in the environment. For many small organisms, and many questions, the steady state or operative temperatures provided by the 'ectotherm' model are fine. But if you want to account for the lag, then you can use the 'transient' models ('onelump', 'onelump_var' and 'twolump_var'), e.g. see http://bioforecasts.science.unimelb.edu.au/app_direct/ectotherm_transient/

It depends on whether you want the operative temperature of a behaving animal. If you want just the potential temperature of the animal sitting in e.g. the open, you can put 'live = 0' then you don't have to worry about changing those parameters you mentioned. Alternatively, you could put 'live = 1' and make the thresholds for activity etc. sufficiently large that they wont ever come into effect, and also make the organism diurnal,  nocturnal and crepusculsar, and that would give you a predicted body temperature that also includes effects of water loss rate and metabolic rate.
All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: How to calculate the water loss in ectotherm?
messages.subject_clean: How to calculate the water loss in ectotherm?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Zhong-wen Jiang,

See attached appendix to
Kearney, M. R., & Porter, W. P. (2004). Mapping the fundamental niche: Physiology, climate, and the distribution of a nocturnal lizard. Ecology, 85(11), 3119–3131.
which has the equations in it. The parameter 'pct_wet' (or the skin resistance to water loss, which can be derived from the 'pct_wet' parameter) is the percentage of the total surface area exposed to air that is acting as a free water surface, with no resistance to water loss. When factoring in the eye, it is assumed that it is a free water surface and this gets added to the effective area for evaporation. You can find more detail in
Pirtle, E. I., Tracy, C. R., & Kearney, M. R. (2019). Hydroregulation – a neglected behavioral response of lizards to climate change? In V. Bels & A. P. Russell (Eds.), Lizard Behavior: Evolutionary and Mechanistic Perspectives. CRC Press.
and
Tracy, C. R. (1976). A model of the dynamic exchanges of water and energy between a terrestrial amphibian and its environment. Ecological Monographs, 46(3), 293–326. (a classic)

All the best,
Mike

The day you're changing is 147, not 269. This is what appears to be causing changes in the relative humidity from what you set it at, which I'll have to dig into a bit more because that shouldn't be happening if air temp in sun and shade are the same.

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike
Context:
Dung beetles were kept outside in 15 cm tubs and starved for 24 hours. Their weight before and after was recorded. This took place in spring, summer, and autumn.
The purpose is to look at thermoregulatory trade offs in relation to seasonal acclimation.

My original questions last month were geared towards a different treatment where the beetles were kept inside, and aren't relevant here.

If burrowing is turned on, does the model assume the ectotherm is always burrowing? I've turned the function off for now and corrected the dates, thank you. Outside from the humidity, the results are within the expected range now!

Hi Alex,

OK thanks for the context. If burrowing is an option, they'll go there when they're not in their active phase, or if temperature are too extreme at the surface. If you allow activity all the time, i.e. nocturnal, diurnal and crepuscular, you'll only see them go underground if conditions are extreme on the surface. Also note that by keeping relative humidity constant and varying temperature, you're actually varying the absolute humidity which I'm guessing is not what you want. Finally, the reason relative humidity was changing was actually because you hadn't changed the shadmet TALOC column and, for the reason just mentioned, the relative humidity was changing. I.e. the model is adjusting humidity for the new air temps in the shade on the assumption that the absolute humidity isn't changing. So there was nothing odd going on in the model (phew!). You just missed putting shadmet rather than metout in your code.

All the best,
Mike
